verdict.rationale: Genesis 3 is narrated in an unbroken wayyiqtol chain (34 consecutive-imperfect verbs, including the eating sequence וַתִּקַּח, וַתֹּאכַל, וַתִּתֵּן, וַיֹּאכַל and the curse and expulsion sequence), the same prose-history verb form that carries the surrounding creation account (Gen 2) and the toledot genealogy (Gen 5, with וַיְחִי and וַיּוֹלֶד treating Adam as the first link of a datable line). Genesis contains zero parable markers (H4912 mashal occurs 0 times), so the text does not flag itself as figurative. Paul argues from this as a punctiliar event: in Rom 5.12 ἁμαρτία εἰσῆλθεν (G1525, aorist V-2AAI-3S) through ἑνὸς ἀνθρώπου, and Rom 5.19 κατεστάθησαν (G2525, aorist passive) constitutes the many as sinners through one man. 1 Cor 15.21 to 22 repeats δι' ἀνθρώπου with ἐν τῷ Ἀδὰμ, where Adam is morphologically tagged a proper noun (N-DSM-P) in strict parallel with Christ. The genuine lexical seam is that the Eden scene mostly calls the agent הָאָדָם, the man with the article (H0120), and only at Gen 3.17 and from Gen 5 onward uses the bare proper name Adam (H0121), which is the lexical room a representative reading exploits, but the narrative grammar and the Adam-Christ parallel keep the historical-agent reading dominant.

scripture.force: The act of disobedience runs in a chain of wayyiqtol consecutive-imperfect verbs, וַתֵּרֶא she saw, וַתִּקַּח she took, וַתֹּאכַל she ate, וַתִּתֵּן she gave, וַיֹּאכַל and he ate, all morphology Vqw, the standard Hebrew prose-narrative form for sequential past events. The grammar frames a concrete event, not a stative or gnomic description.

Here the agent is named with the bare proper noun וּלְאָדָם, morph Np, the first proper-name use inside the scene, addressed in the second person שָׁמַעְתָּ you listened. The curse formula אֲרוּרָה הָאֲדָמָה בַּעֲבוּרֶךָ, cursed is the ground on your account, with H0779 arar, ties the ground's corruption directly to one particular agent's prior act.

The serpent הַנָּחָשׁ is tagged article plus common noun, Td/Ncmsa, an ordinary animate subject inside the narrative clause. The text does not lexically mark it as a symbol. Whether it is read figuratively is an interpretive move the morphology neither demands nor flags, which is part of the genuine room some readers use.

The toledot heading זֶה סֵפֶר תּוֹלְדֹת אָדָם, the book of the generations of Adam (H0121 Np), folds Adam into the same genealogical register as the later patriarchs, carried by וַיְחִי he lived and וַיּוֹלֶד he begot. The genealogy treats Adam as the datable first link of a real line, the same verb form found across the rest of Genesis history.

δι' ἑνὸς ἀνθρώπου ἡ ἁμαρτία εἰς τὸν κόσμον εἰσῆλθεν. The verb εἰσῆλθεν is G1525 parsed V-2AAI-3S, second aorist active indicative, a punctiliar single entry-point, not a present or imperfect describing an ongoing condition. καὶ οὕτως εἰς πάντας ἀνθρώπους ὁ θάνατος διῆλθεν (G1330, also aorist), ἐφ' ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον (G0264, aorist), distributes the consequence universally from that one act.

ἐβασίλευσεν ὁ θάνατος ἀπὸ Ἀδὰμ μέχρι Μωϋσέως. The two named termini Adam and Moses place Adam on the same historical plane as Moses, a datable person. τύπος τοῦ μέλλοντος then casts Adam as the typological counterpart of the coming one.

δι' ἑνὸς παραπτώματος εἰς πάντας ἀνθρώπους εἰς κατάκριμα. A singular trespass, genitive of cause, yields a global verdict, εἰς πάντας ἀνθρώπους, set symmetrically against δι' ἑνὸς δικαιώματος, one act of righteousness.

διὰ τῆς παρακοῆς τοῦ ἑνὸς ἀνθρώπου ἁμαρτωλοὶ κατεστάθησαν οἱ πολλοί. The verb κατεστάθησαν is G2525 parsed V-API-3P, aorist passive indicative, constituting the many as sinners on the basis of one man's disobedience. The future κατασταθήσονται mirrors it for the one man's obedience, a causal constitution, not a mere ethical example.
τῇ ματαιότητι ἡ κτίσις ὑπετάγη. The aorist passive ὑπετάγη plus οὐχ ἑκοῦσα marks a definite past subjection of creation, consonant with the curse on the ground at Gen 3.17.
ἀπὸ τῆς δουλείας τῆς φθορᾶς. Creation is in bondage to corruption awaiting liberation, presupposing a real prior fall, not merely an inherent flaw.
συστενάζει καὶ συνωδίνει πᾶσα ἡ κτίσις ἄχρι τοῦ νῦν. A durative present plus ἄχρι τοῦ νῦν, until now, locates the groaning on a timeline that reaches back to an originating event.

ἐπειδὴ γὰρ δι' ἀνθρώπου θάνατος, καὶ δι' ἀνθρώπου ἀνάστασις νεκρῶν. The δι' ἀνθρώπου to δι' ἀνθρώπου parallel requires both sides to be referents of the same kind, that is real persons, since the resurrection side is unambiguously a historical person.

ὥσπερ γὰρ ἐν τῷ Ἀδὰμ πάντες ἀποθνῄσκουσιν, οὕτως καὶ ἐν τῷ Χριστῷ πάντες ζῳοποιηθήσονται. Ἀδάμ is morphologically tagged N-DSM-P, a proper personal noun, exactly parallel to Χριστῷ. The ἐν preposition signals corporate-representative incorporation, and the equal tagging of both heads resists treating one as a person and the other as an abstraction.

ἐγένετο ὁ πρῶτος ἄνθρωπος Ἀδὰμ εἰς ψυχὴν ζῶσαν. Adam is tagged N-NSM-P, proper noun, the first man, set against ὁ ἔσχατος Ἀδάμ, the last Adam. The first-and-last bracketing treats both as concrete persons heading their respective humanities.

complicating_texts.resolution: The relative clause ἐφ' ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον has been read either causally, because all sinned, or as a relative, in whom all sinned. Either reading still anchors universal death to one man's act, since the prior clause already attributes the entry of sin and death to ἑνὸς ἀνθρώπου through the aorist εἰσῆλθεν, and εἰς πάντας ἀνθρώπους then generalizes it. The single historical entry-point is the lexical anchor regardless of which gloss is preferred.

ἁμαρτία δὲ οὐκ ἐλλογεῖται μὴ ὄντος νόμου notes that sin is not reckoned where there is no law, yet v.14 says ἐβασίλευσεν ὁ θάνατος ἀπὸ Ἀδὰμ μέχρι Μωϋσέως over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam's transgression. The text resolves this by tying the universal reign of death to Adam's original transgression rather than to each individual's own law-breaking, which strengthens rather than weakens the one-event reading.

The narrative furniture of the scene, the speaking serpent הַנָּחָשׁ and the named trees, is what a figurative or archetypal reading leans on. Lexically the serpent is tagged only article plus common noun, an ordinary clause subject, and Genesis contains zero parable markers (H4912 mashal occurs 0 times in the book). The morphology neither flags nor forbids a symbolic reading of these elements, so this remains a real but limited interpretive seam rather than a textual signal that overturns the narrative-history grammar.

Inside the Eden scene the agent is overwhelmingly called הָאָדָם, the man with the definite article (H0120, the appellative, 16 times in Gen 2 and 7 in Gen 3), and only at Gen 3.17 and from Gen 5.1 onward does the bare proper name אָדָם appear (H0121, Np). This article-bearing appellative is the strongest lexical basis for a representative or every-person reading. It is addressed but not fully dissolved by the words alone, because the same chapters also use the proper name and the Gen 5 toledot genealogy treats Adam as a datable individual, so the appellative cannot be pressed into a purely generic sense across the whole chain.

variant_units_examined.note: Some witnesses are reported to omit μή before ἁμαρτήσαντας. Either reading preserves Adam and Moses as the historical termini of death's reign and leaves the one-event verdict intact.
Minor article and word-order variation around θάνατος does not touch the δι' ἀνθρώπου to δι' ἀνθρώπου parallel between the two heads.

variants.note: Anchor verses in Romans 5, Romans 8, and 1 Corinthians 15 fall outside the ingested CBGM window, which covers only 3 John. Variant notes here rest on standard apparatus traces, not on published ECM data, so they are recorded as shadow only.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Genesis 3 carries 34 wayyiqtol consecutive-imperfect verbs, the standard Hebrew prose-history form, continuous with the surrounding creation account and the Gen 5 toledot genealogy, and Genesis uses no parable marker. Read by its own grammar the chapter narrates a sequence of real past events.

Inside the Eden scene the agent is named overwhelmingly as הָאָדָם, the man with the article (H0120), an appellative that can read as humanity as such, and the scene includes a speaking serpent and symbolic trees that the morphology does not lexically mark as literal. On this lens the chapter is a true-but-representative portrait of every person's turning from God, told in narrative dress. This reading is grammatically possible for the Eden scene taken in isolation, which is why it is recorded fairly.

ἑνὸς ἀνθρώπου in Rom 5 and ἐν τῷ Ἀδὰμ in 1 Cor 15.22 read Adam as a covenant head whose single act yields a universal verdict on those represented in him, with κατεστάθησαν marking a constitutive, not merely exemplary, relation.

Adam is tagged a proper noun (N-DSM-P, N-NSM-P) in exact parallel with Christ in 1 Cor 15.21 to 22 and 45, and called τύπος τοῦ μέλλοντος in Rom 5.14. The parallel resists a category mismatch where one head is a person and the other an abstraction, which pulls the archetypal reading back toward a real Adam at the canon level.

The Gen 3 to Rom 5 to Rom 8 to 1 Cor 15 chain treats Adam's act, creation's bondage under φθορά, and Christ's resurrection as nodes on one timeline marked by aorists and the ἄχρι τοῦ νῦν of Rom 8.22. The arc requires a real originating event.

hermeneutics.notes: Pan-canonical anchor across Torah narrative and Pauline epistles. The honest tension is internal to the Hebrew: the Eden scene favors the article-bearing appellative הָאָדָם while the toledot and Paul favor the proper name and proper-noun tagging. The Adam-Christ typology is structurally load-bearing in both Rom 5 and 1 Cor 15 and tends to settle the canon-level reading toward a historical Adam.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: There was a definite originating disobedience by the first human in primeval history, with consequences of sin, death, and corruption reaching humanity and the created order.
stem_audit.notes: The stem's phrase covenant head encodes a federal-headship mechanism, and plunging humanity and the created order encodes the scope claim. The neutralized form keeps the historical-event claim and the universal-consequence claim while leaving the representational mechanism (federal, seminal, or representative) a downstream question. The verdict is rendered on the original stem. affirms is unchanged from the prior file; the lexical work confirms it rather than forcing a flip.

lay_summary: The words decide this in two layers. In Genesis 3 the story runs through a long chain of Hebrew verbs in the form Hebrew uses for sequential past events, the same verb form that carries the creation account just before it and the family-tree history of chapter 5 just after it, where Adam heads a line of people who lived and had children. She saw, she took, she ate, she gave, he ate, then the ground is cursed because of one named agent. The book never uses its word for parable, so the text does not flag itself as a fable. Paul then treats this as a single dated event. He says sin entered the world through one man, and the verb entered is a one-time past-tense verb, a single doorway, not an ongoing mood. He says one man's disobedience made the many sinners, again a settled past action, not a bad example. In Romans 8 he stretches the damage to all creation, subjected to futility and groaning until now, words that point back to a real starting point. In First Corinthians 15 he sets death through a man against resurrection through a man, and tags Adam grammatically as a proper personal name, exactly the way he tags Christ, so the parallel only works if both are real persons. There is one honest seam in the words. Inside the garden scene the agent is mostly called the man, with the word the, which can read as humanity in general, and the talking serpent and the trees are not labeled as symbols. That is the room a representative reading uses. But the narrative grammar, the genealogy that counts Adam as a datable ancestor, and the proper-name parallel with Christ keep the historical-event reading dominant. So the proposition stands, with high confidence, on the words alone.
